The request's bearer credential is the session cookie's token, which

`Authorization` header of its own.

nodes_changed.name: attach_browser_caller
nodes_changed.signature: pub(crate) async fn attach_browser_caller( State(state): State<AppState>, mut request: Request, next: Next, ) -> Response
nodes_changed.doc:
Reads the session cookie, re-validates its access token against the

issuer's keys, and attaches the resulting [`CallerIdentity`] to the

request. A cookie that no longer validates is cleared rather than

honored; without a cookie, or without browser sign-in configured, the

request passes through anonymous.

nodes_changed.name: present_session_token
nodes_changed.signature: pub(crate) fn present_session_token( headers: &mut axum::http::HeaderMap, access_token: &str, ) -> Option<SessionBearer>
nodes_changed.doc:
Presents the session's access token as the request's bearer credential,

unless the request already carries one.



The browser's own RPC calls (connect-web, same origin) carry the session

cookie and no `Authorization` header. The shell's RPC enforcement point

and the hosts it forwards to verify bearer tokens, so without this a

signed-in person's every RPC would be refused as anonymous. The token is

the one the session already validated above, minted for the

`[auth.browser]` audience -- which every profile that signs browsers in

sets equal to `[auth.rpc]`'s, and a topology test holds them together.

An explicit header wins: a CLI or a test presenting its own token is

asking as itself.



Returns [`SessionBearer`] when it presented the token, for the request's

extensions: the RPC guard (`transport::rpc_csrf`) checks that a request

whose credential is the cookie came from one of the shell's own pages.

an explicit identity rather than whatever the environment holds.

nodes_changed.name: from_topology

nodes_changed.doc:
Builds both enforcement points, once, from the environment and what

the topology's `[auth.rpc]` declares, under the requirement of the

resolved deployment environment.



The RPC surface and the metadata-admin plane both take `[auth.rpc]`,

behind the environment in `local` and alone elsewhere, as the hosts

do. The plane verifies a token on every method it serves, drive's

included: drive calls it as the workload `causeway-drive-ops` with a

token its issuer signed, and no shared secret reaches it

(RFD-krvga4f3).



What this returns is the only authentication the shell has. The

router, the application state and through it every metadata-ops

route are handed it, so a route cannot authorize by settings this

did not validate, and a misconfiguration stops startup here instead

of failing a first request (RFD-j1jabh49).



# Errors



Returns every problem with either, naming the settings to fix.

node.doc:
A person from the directory calling the shell with a token an

in-process Mokta minted, for a test that needs an authenticated caller.



It replaces the test persona every caller once was: the shell verifies

the token as it would any other, and the caller's subject and groups are

the directory's (RFD-krvga4f3). Keep it alive for the test: dropping it

stops the issuer whose keys the shell fetches.

node.name: answer
node.signature: async fn answer( State(origins): State<Arc<AllowedOrigins>>, request: Request, next: Next, ) -> Response
node.doc:
Answers a request under an allow-list.



A preflight is answered here and never reaches a route: for an allowed

origin with that origin, credentials and what it may send; for any

other with nothing, which the browser reads as a refusal. Any other

request runs, and only an allowed origin's answer carries that origin

and credentials. Every answer varies by origin, so no cache hands one

origin's answer to another.

node.name: guard
node.signature: pub(super) async fn guard(State(state): State<AppState>, req: Request, next: Next) -> Response
node.doc:
Deny requests to surfaces the deployment profile disables.



This is the authoritative access control for the `microsite-basic` profile:

hiding a CTA is cosmetic; this denies the route even on a direct URL,

bookmark, or crawl. A disabled surface answers `303 → /` (See Other) so a stray link

lands on the public home rather than an error (ADR 0017 §3).



One central layer covers all three gated groups rather than a per-handler

check, so coverage does not depend on remembering to gate each new page.

The gates fail open — a flag-evaluation hiccup serves the route.

Determination 7: an autonomous agent may take no stuck-work action.



The surface's actions all enter through the plane check, whose policy

request carries `AI_AUTONOMOUS_PROHIBITED`, so the refusal is one

rule rather than a check repeated in five handlers. An operator with

the same scopes passes the same door.

The pending login is a cookie on the host the browser asked, and Mokta
returns to SHELL_ORIGIN: a browser on `localhost` would reach the callback
without it ("no sign-in is in progress in this browser"), so its login
moves to the callback's origin before anything is set.
